title: Deque
short: A line you can add to or take from at both ends.
what: A deque (said "deck") is a double-ended queue. You can add or remove items at the front and at the back, each in one step. It can also hold a fixed number of items and drop the oldest when a new one arrives.
analogy: A train where carriages can be hooked on or off at either end, but never in the middle.

frames.label: d
frames.say: d = deque([2, 3, 4]). Both ends are open for adding and removing.

frames.label: d
frames.say: d.appendleft(1) puts 1 at the front. On a list, insert(0, 1) would shift every item; here nothing moves.

frames.label: d
frames.say: d.append(5) adds at the back, the same as on a list.

frames.label: d
frames.say: d.popleft() takes 1 from the front and d.pop() takes 5 from the back. Both are O(1).

frames.label: recent, maxlen=3
frames.say: A second deque, made with maxlen=3, keeps only the 3 newest items. It is full with 2, 3, 4.

frames.label: recent, maxlen=3
frames.say: append(6) on a full deque pushes the oldest item, 2, out of the front by itself.

frames.label: recent, maxlen=3
frames.say: Now it holds the last 3 values: 3, 4, 6. Handy for "the last k events" and moving windows.

when: Add or remove at both ends
Keep only the last k items
python:
from collections import deque

d = deque([2, 3, 4])
d.appendleft(1)
d.append(5)
print(d)
print(d.popleft(), d.pop())

recent = deque([2, 3, 4], maxlen=3)
recent.append(6)
print(recent)
print(recent[0], recent[-1])
cost: Add or remove at either end
watch: Reading the middle with d[i] walks to it, so it is slow. Use a list if you index a lot.
Slices like d[1:3] fail. Convert with list(d) first.
With maxlen, items fall off the other end without any warning.
